newsitem.title: USA: Anti-terrorism bill too rigid, White House says.
newsitem.headline: Anti-terrorism bill too rigid, White House says.

text.p: A House of Representatives panel's bill to make the administration enforce a U.S. ban on financial transactions with governments viewed as supporting terrorism would have harmful consequences, Clinton administration officials said on Tuesday.
The Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act passed in 1996 prohibited financial transactions with North Korea, Cuba, Libya, Iran, Iraq, Sudan and Syria.

The administration treated Sudan and Syria less severely because they were seen as cooperating in some areas. But several members of a House Judiciary subcommittee said they wanted legislation to make the administration enforce the ban uniformly, extending it to Sudan and Syria.
They also charged that the administration gutted a similar law through regulations it wrote in 1996, forcing the subcommittee to bring up another bill this year.
"I've rarely seen an effort that is so blatant to subvert the intent of Congress. I think you should be ashamed of these regulations," Georgia Republican Bob Barr said at a hearing.

The House bill would bar almost all financial transactions between U.S. entities and governments that are on the U.S. list of terrorist-supporting governments and strip the White House of discretion over how the law is administered.
Missouri Republican Sen. John Ashcroft introduced a similar bill in the Senate on Tuesday.
At a hearing on the House bill, administration officials said it would make the law too rigid to be effective and could have unintended consequences that would impair U.S. efforts to fight terrorism.
"Flexibility in designing specific measures is vital to the success of sanctions," William Ramsey, deputy assistant secretary of state for energy, sanctions and commodities, said.

The State Department coordinator for counter-terrorism, Philip Wilcox Jr., said Sudan and Syria were not as flagrant violators as others on the list and have been cooperative in some areas. Harsher sanctions could imperil some advances, such as peace efforts between Syria and Israel, he said.

The House panel's bill also could raise other problems, Ramsey said, such as hampering assistance to support democracy and humanitarian efforts in these countries, halting repatriation from North Korea of U.S. soldiers who died in the Korean War, halting U.S. participation in the United Nations-backed oil-for-food deal for Iraq and hampering the orderly, legal migration of Cubans to the United States.
